The orbit here is crowded with junk traffic and idle sats, a forgotten ring of hardware looping a world nobody bothers to check twice. I have been sitting in this cramped berth on The Den long enough to know why nobody volunteers for this posting. The schematic is wrong in all the same ways the patrol logs were: tiny offsets, repeated notations, a cluster of emergency waypoints quietly dragged along a single, invisible line through space. I am still shaking dust out of my hair from this bunker, and the consoles are older than half the patrol grid, but they still know how to keep a secret. Some of the techs back in the dive swear they saw it slip past on a dead transponder; others say it is all barroom exaggeration. Either way, the next piece of this mess is sitting in a silent UC hulk, waiting for someone brave or desperate enough to board it.

Out here, among rusted hulls and half gutted frames, Deadlock is surrounded by the language he understands best; every twisted beam and stripped Grav Drive mount is a tool he has already weighed and repurposed in his head. The fields look like any other out on the fringe  tilled soil, tired fences, a farmhouse patched more with hope than credits. That is why this place matters. No one logs a relay out here by mistake; an asteroid field this thin, this far from any declared corridor, exists to lose signals, not anchor them, which is exactly why someone like Luna would lace her work through its static. The rocks and dust give cover to whatever she tested first, the bad corridors and half-finished vanish routes that never made it onto official charts, and to anyone now hired to erase those traces before a hunter can read them. Out in this drift, there is no jurisdiction, no flight control, only the raw noise of grav drives and broken stone, and somewhere inside that noise is the pattern she has been refining since her first ship went missing. Stories about a ghost in the traffic have passed from LIST clerks to GalBank pilots and bar-front fixers, picking up new details every retelling, but the only solid things so far were a protection escort whose route logs did not match its manifest and whispers that certain beacons in dead space repeat the same warped checksum, like an echo waiting for someone stubborn enough to chase it.

HM-6310 is still out there, hanging between beacons like a bad thought no one wants to finish. I caught its ID in a rundown dockside bar, buried in a spacer s story he swore was just a joke. Dead Navy hull, clean cuts in the comms, no scorch marks from a boarding, no beacon loop. Just silence, and a notation buried three menus deep that says "operational loss" in the kind of language auditors use when they do not want to know more.  \n\nWhat sticks with me is not the ship itself, it is the pattern around it. Convoys rerouted for "efficiency," escorts arriving a little late, patrols shifted one sector over for reasons that sound reasonable until you realize they always leave one lane thin. Then something disappears and everybody shrugs and blames raiders, or equipment, or bad luck. Nobody ever mentions the matching blackout windows or the way records get neater the closer you get to New Atlantis. Every time I bring it up, people laugh it off too fast, like they are afraid if they stop joking the truth will land somewhere between cowardice and calculation.

Calen Rourke here, logging this before someone decides it is inconvenient and wipes the drive clean. The module is dead quiet, just fans and my own breathing, but the consoles tell a louder story than most captains ever will. I traced the data forks like any good thief would trace a payout, following the jumps where they should not bend, the packets that detoured through places no contract mentioned. Every time the trail went fuzzy, the same ship ID kept reappearing in scrubbed access notes and half-redacted audit flags from the Trade Authority. Someone thought routing that much traffic through a single cargo hauler was subtle, that if they buried it in routine freight no one would notice. Maybe they were right, for a while. But the broken beacon logs we pulled near the outer marker, the whispers in Neon's lower levels about ghost routes, and that LIST emergency broadcast everyone pretends not to remember, they all point back to the same thing: a cargo ship running too many "lucky" jumps and a pilot whose name keeps getting spoken in a lower voice every time.

Ryujin's tower would be the tidy cut. Climate control, polished stone, security guards who pretend they do not see what their employers pay to hide. If I go there, I am not just chasing a rogue navigator, I am kicking the legs out from under whatever board signed off on these experiments. Paper trails, scrubbed payouts, research budgets rewritten into alibis. It is cleaner work, at least on the surface, but stepping into that building means treating this like a crime of suits, not just one woman weaponizing math.\n\nThe listening post is the opposite end of the spectrum raw sky, dead hardware, mercs instead of receptionists. Hotel Hardstrike holding the line over repurposed UC ears, guarding beacon logs no one wants to admit still exist. If I go there first, I am betting that the truth is buried in noise and old war habits, not balance sheets. More guns, fewer lawyers. One path puts me in boardrooms and back channels, the other drops me in a forgotten bunker with mercenaries paid to ask no questions. Either way, the same signature keeps surfacing in the data.

The empty barracks still hum with recycled air and old orders, a forgotten outpost built to outlast the Colony War and then quietly abandoned when the treaties came. Rivet chose this place because no one counts the dead here anymore, and because the walls are already wired for controlled demolitions and silent drills; it is the perfect frame to cut apart and vanish inside. His grav logs, stolen drives, and the star map that ties every gutted wreck together will be staged to jump from here, slipping past Freestar patrol routes and UC scrutiny alike. If he succeeds, the pattern he has been tracing in secret will move beyond anyone's reach, along with the last unedited record of what really happened in those forgotten battles. From the frozen carcass in deep space where a stranded cutter dropped Rivet's name, to the quiet farm where Waggoner soil hid Deimos-marked scrap, to the garrison stripped along precise load-bearing seams, every step has pointed to one hand testing structures, erasing witnesses, and following that same impossible signal through the wreckage.

If I head for the Clinic, I go where the damage is catalogued and given names. Every grav-burned pilot, every fractured mind from a bad jump, all quietly stored behind polite smiles and redacted reports. If his work ever brushed flesh, it is written there in nerve maps and scar tissue. The risk is eyes on me from every authority that cares about their reputation, but the payoff is simple and sharp: I might finally see what his numbers do to real people instead of empty hulls.\n\nIf I drop to the old recon hide, I am chasing the first honest look at how he slips through a net designed to catch everything. The bunker is dead on paper, but its recorders were built to watch without blinking, and they do not care whose career gets ruined by what they saw. Less politics, more ghosts: cold air, old UC hardware, and maybe one uncut sequence of a ship walking between sensor sweeps like it knows where the blind spots live. One path walks me into crowded corridors and whispered testimonies; the other into dust, silence, and raw telemetry. Either way, his shadow is waiting.

I have been chasing this name in the margins for months now and I am still not sure if it belongs to a person, a program, or just the way crews talk when they do not want to say what they really mean. Every time a run threads between storms that were not on the forecast, somebody shrugs and jokes that "someone upstairs has a good broker," and the room gets just a shade quieter. I am sitting in the mess of this Alliance cutter now, listening to its empty hull tick and cool, trying to piece together how a ship built to haul bounty contracts ended up holding what looks more like a weather ledger than a job list. No one left a clean record; just half-finished notes, rerouted payments, corridors of fog that keep matching the same three or four departure points. All I know for sure is that it started on a dustball outpost with cargo that should have been delayed by a week of rain and was not, then a hunter's wreck drifting way off course with storm data in its black box, then manifests from a factory town whose harvests refused to line up with their own climate reports.

I came back to this rock because the noise would not shut up. You stand on the ridge and the wind is the only thing you hear, but jack into the local relay and it is like listening to a hoarder's attic: half-deleted pings, orphaned status codes, messages queued for recipients who have been dead a decade. This place should have been swept clean when the UC pulled their survey drones. It was not. Somebody skipped a step, or pretended to, and whatever he pushed through the buffer back then got caught in the same neglect.\n\nI keep replaying a fragment, a routing tag that does not match any registered ship, pulsing at intervals too regular to be ghost data. The dead agent's scribbled coordinates, that dataslate I bought off a frightened farmer, even the story about armed escorts circling a field that glowed after dark, they all bend toward the same name. Feels like everyone saw a piece and shrugged, too busy or too scared to add it up. Now I am standing in the middle of what they overlooked, wondering how long this signal has been waiting for someone to finally notice.

Places like The Clinic are supposed to scrub the blood off history, pin it behind glass with a comforting plaque, and call that healing. That is why the trail bends here: if anyone tried to turn a battlefield horror into a neat case study, it would be the station that survived a war by changing hands instead of course. Somewhere in its curated corridors there will be a sanitized version of what happened at that garrison, and tucked behind that, the parts the UC was glad to misplace and Freestar has no incentive to dig up. Staff whisper different stories when they think no one is listening; some fear what an unedited record might stir up, others like the safety that comes from not asking questions.  \nUp to now, the path has been fragments and contradictions: a stray slate on a forgotten rock, a derelict patrol ship still following half-erased orders, conflicting mentions of the same medic in logs that should never overlap. Everything points back to one incident no one wants to own, and a man who walked out of it still answering to commands nobody remembers signing.

I am writing this before I lose my nerve and toss that slate back into the crate where I found it. Out here the manifests are still smeared in oil and bad handwriting, but the numbers are too neat around that one tug. Wrong hull ID, wrong routing stamp, and three different initials "fixing" the same mistake. I asked the clerk on duty who changed it; she swore she only copied what came from Gagarin. The yard boss said he signed off because a UC rep vouched for it. The rep, when I finally reached him on a laggy channel, insisted the request came from "higher up" and cut the call. Nobody owns the decision, but they all heard it from someone else first.\n\nI keep thinking about that cutter and the way its line just stops, replaced by a phantom courier that never shows on any legitimate docket. First it was a rumor from a hauler who swore a whole crew vanished off Titan. Then it was a half-burned name on a memorial wall. Now it is my own pen hovering over a ledger, deciding whether to pretend I did not see a ship quietly pushed into a graveyard route that should not exist.

The Deserted Relay Station hangs at the edge of the system like a dead nerve in the grav lattice, perfectly placed where old UC traffic once converged and where Vector can now listen to every tremor in the lanes. Its dishes have been twisted into a spider's web of jury-rigged antennas, feeding his stolen diagnostics and anomaly models into a humming core that treats the whole sector as a laboratory. Here, at the intersection of abandoned infrastructure and unstable readings, he can attempt the final proof he has been chasing since the testbed freighter died, a localized grav twitch big enough to force the truth into the open or tear this orbit apart. A misrouted UC maintenance order, an unsigned transfer request in New Atlantis, and a delayed pirate intercept have all nudged this confrontation here, now. Earlier, the quiet failures at the research site, the corrupted logs in high orbit, and the redacted disputes buried in Calyx files all traced the same pattern of staged "accidents" and missing data, pointing to the same exhausted analyst running out of places to hide.

I came up here to babysit a bank of half-dead sensors and drink bad coffee, not to stumble over someone else's ghost trail. The hut looks abandoned unless you know where to listen; under the wind and the creaking mast there is this steady tick of relays, software from three revisions ago still chewing on sky and ground like nobody ever told it the war was over. Half the crew cycles through, signs the maintenance sheet, never checks what the system is actually flagging. Today I dug into the ignored queue, the one that has been auto-filing anomalies as "atmospherics" for years, and there it was: a clean thermal line knifing across the ridge, too straight for weather, too smooth for wildlife, logged and time-stamped by a process nobody remembers writing. I asked around in town, and suddenly everybody's memory got real convenient; the sheriff recalls a storm, the pilot remembers "instrument noise," the bartender swears the night was quiet. The only thing not lying to me is this forgotten code, still doing its job long after the people who trusted it stopped paying attention.

The farm is the first wound on the map, a place the banks wrote off and the locals forgot, which makes it perfect for hiding the kind of record no one wants audited. Its fields lie fallow under a thin sky, but the power feed to the main house still hums, and there are fresh boot tracks in the dust that do not belong to settlers. Uniform Blackguard watch the place with the stiff patience of contractors told to guard something they are not allowed to open, their black-and-white marks stark against sun-bleached siding; whatever is on that farm terminal, it scared someone enough to pay for silence. In town, stories about the foreclosure and the family who vanished never quite match, and every time the argument starts over who was at fault, it ends in a shrug and a change of subject, like everybody agreed not to dig any deeper. So far the trail is thin but steady: a dead spacer clutching stolen audit clips, a homestead that settled its debts after it was already empty, and scattered whispers that the same unseen hand keeps touching accounts from Akila to forgotten LIST rocks.

I am not supposed to be working this, not officially. I am just the deputy they park in the field trailer to shuffle reports and pretend the border is quiet. But yesterday, while I was cleaning up an old convoy case, I pulled the raw traffic burst the UC shared with us for "coordination." Someone sliced our copy sloppily. A patch of static where their data shows a clean handoff, a time stamp that does not line up with engine burn logs, and a relay ID that should have been retired cycles ago.\n\nWhoever scrubbed it did it in a hurry and trusted nobody would look twice. They were almost right. I cross-checked that relay ID against older incidents and found it echoing behind three different "navigation failures," always the same forgotten listening post drifting just off the main corridor. The captains who survived keep blaming cheap charts or bad luck, and command is happy to let them. I have forwarded nothing yet. All I know is that the same interference that bent the buoy you are chasing once bounced through that dead UC ear, and every time it did, another convoy went dark.

I am recording this from the shack before I lose my nerve and sell the whole lot to the highest bidder. The walls here sweat condensation and stolen power, a tangle of rusted antennae and half-burnt routers humming on frequencies no sane port authority checks anymore. That is why her traffic washed up on my doorstep.  \n\nIt did not come as some grand revelation. Just a double-echo in the bands, two identical convoys that never existed on any manifest, both vanishing into a dead patch where no one flies unless they have to. I followed the ghosts back through weeks of chatter, past Crimson Fleet dead-drops and Ryujin side channels, until every route rebounded off the same cold coordinate string. Spacers in back rooms keep saying Deadchannel is a myth, or a hero, or a corporate hit piece, depending on who owes who, but every retelling shaves a little truth away. The raw recordings I pulled do not care about stories. They all point to the same place the next relay in her chain, a forgotten UC node floating in the dark, where the signals go silent and the lies stop being rumors.

Neon's skyline is a liar's chorus, but the rooftops hum with the truth underneath it. Up there, routes are sold between drinks, fees are laundered through private pads, and people talk more freely when they think the wind will carry their secrets away. If Vector ever bragged, even by accident, it was probably in the shadow of the Span, his coordinates traded like ghost stories between smugglers and corporate fixers. Chasing that thread means wading into gossip, greasing palms, and listening hard for one voice that talks in numbers instead of names.\n\nThe relay bunker is different. No noise, no drinks, just machines that never learned how to lie. Someone pulled atmospheric traces there and saw something they should not have, then quietly stepped off the grid. The logs they left behind read the same way every time: the same anomaly, the same path through restricted sky. Following that line means trusting cold data over street talk, digging into whatever is riding inside that forgotten SysDef hull and hoping the people who were supposed to clean this up are not still watching.

I am writing this where no one can look over my shoulder. Out here the stars are too bright and the air is too thin for comfort, but at least the only ears are mine. I pulled the last three months of sensor sweeps from the patrol grid, buried behind routine smuggling alerts and meteor warnings. There is a pattern in the noise, a faint smear of grav interference that keeps showing up in the same narrow band of orbit. It is not on any flight plan, but it pulses with the same timing as those "isolated malfunctions" command keeps renaming.\n\nWhen I tried to bring it up in the ready room, the room went quiet in that careful way. Nobody told me I was wrong, nobody asked to see the data. They just found somewhere else to look. That is how I know I am close. The signature climbs out from the blind side of this rock and vanishes right where a derelict comms platform went missing six years ago. First the dead cache, then the jump-scarred freighter, now a grav shadow in empty orbit, all sharing the same geometry. Whatever she is doing, she is walking the same invisible line every time.

I am recording this before I lose the nerve to listen to my own voice.

The bunker is colder than outside. Systems half-dead, dust on every console, like nobody has breathed in here since the last war. I jacked into the relay expecting dead air and junk packets, but the patrol grid was still whispering to itself, looping old atmospheric scans like a nervous habit. Buried in all that static, the same transponder ghost kept reappearing over the border, slipping through restricted airspace and vanishing right over the old barracks line. No alarms, no flags, just quietly filed away and forgotten. Somebody trusted the summaries and never looked at the raw feed again.

I pulled the logs myself, traced the drift pattern, and there it was: a ship riding the same corridor, again and again, like it knew exactly where the blind spot lived. Every course correction points back to those ruined barracks outside Akila, like they are using the ghosts of old casualty reports as cover. Feels like this has been happening for years, hiding in full sight of everyone who stopped paying attention.

The Underbelly trail feels like chasing whispers through a power grid. If Vector is bleeding off city juice to push those impossible jumps, somebody down there has seen the lights flicker at the wrong time. It will mean leaning on coil crews and Ghost Coil hangers-on, parsing shrugs and half-finished sentences until a pattern finally shakes loose. Low light, close quarters, every conversation a chance to step on Ryujin toes or some local gang's territory, but if I crack their work logs I might see when and where his ship plugs into Neon's heartbeat.\n\nThe wreck in orbit is colder, simpler, and maybe more honest. Steel remembers what people would rather argue about, and those scorched plates are a flight recorder carved in metal. Follow the twist in the struts, map the angle of that sideways burn, and I could pin down the corridor he is been rehearsing, the direction he keeps trying to tear open. It is riskier in different ways: dead space, thin cover, and anyone else hunting these ghost jumps might be watching the same drifting grave, waiting to see who comes to read its scars.

Should have burned the cache the first night. It was meant to be a quick skim while the relay was quiet check a few flagged packets, flip them for drink money, forget the rest. Then I saw the pattern tucked under all the spacer noise and Crimson chatter the same correction marks, same timing gaps, slipping through systems that do not share charts. I told myself I would just hold onto one clean slice, something I could trade if the wrong people ever decided I knew too much. That was the oversight. Word got around that I "had Vector on tape." Now I have captains leaning on my door and bounty types sniffing the air like they can smell the bits. I traced one of her cleaner jumps riding a Vanguard transponder they should not have been anywhere near the anomaly she used, but there they were, drive singing almost the same tune as her freelance runs. Whatever she is doing, she has their hardware in her hands, even if they pretend otherwise. From that little corporate lab to this shack, every scrap says the next solid piece of her trail is locked in a dead navy hull that never made it home.

I did not like coming back to this hole in the rock. The cavern sweats fuel and cold air, and the quartermaster counts crates like they are sins he will never confess. Still, credits loosened his tongue, a little. He never said her name, not once, but his eyes kept flicking to the ceiling, like something could be listening through stone.  

The manifests he finally showed me were scrubbed, but the nav offsets were wrong in a very particular way, a familiar kink in the numbers. Buried in the timing of those jumps is a rendezvous pattern that only resolves if you project it off-world, just above this system's gravity well.  

So the trail now runs: that forgotten outpost where someone left a data crumb, the mismatched docking records tied to a hauler in Neon, and a smuggler here who moved war junk on a schedule that matches neither trade lanes nor patrol sweeps. Three points on a curve that bends up into empty orbit, where someone has been hiding messages in the spaces between official routes, and everyone who has seen it only talks about it in lowered voices, if they talk at all.

I keep replaying the last clean jump in my head, trying to remember if anything felt wrong. On the scopes it was textbook smooth approach, green lights from the UC tower, a corridor plotted so tight you could shave with it. Nobody questioned it. Why would they We all trust those vectors like gravity.

Then the stories started trickling in, always secondhand. A cousin of a hauler swore a freighter vanished on the same track, but his captain heard it from a GalBank adjuster who blamed pirates. A bartender in New Atlantis told me of a courier that never docked, and she swore she heard it from a Vanguard pilot. Every time I leaned in, they leaned back, said someone else knew more, that they were just passing it along.

Now I am standing on CM-1304, UC crest still stamped over the airlock, and the logs do not match the bodies. The recorded course is pristine, the telemetry too clean, like someone scrubbed out the struggle and left only the math. Whoever laid these lanes knew exactly where they bent, and everyone who ever touched them swears they only heard the warning from someone else.

Gagarin is the safer kind of rotten. Paper trails, nervous clerks, off-world suits pretending not to see the dust caking their server racks. If she sold the sky to anyone, the proof is probably humming away in those annex stacks, buried under invoices and falsified maintenance reports. Walking in means talking to people, peeling back corporate lies one spreadsheet at a time, maybe finding out who paid her and why they needed the storms moved. It feels like the path to answers that end up in a tribunal, not a morgue.\n\nThat wreck out in the orbital junk-ring is another story. No witnesses, no politics, just scorched metal quietly stitching together every odd reading I have chased so far. If that telemetry really is the hinge in her pattern, cracking it open might finally show where all these altered skies converge next. But the kind of people who use dead satellites as waypoints do not like being seen, and if she has built herself a back door through obsolete UC hardware, following it means stepping into a place she has been shaping, pressure line by pressure line, for a very long time.

No court, no committee, would ever authorize a strike here, which is why he chose it; this forgotten Deimos scrapyard is where the company buried its mistakes under rust, slag, and sealed manifests, then agreed to never speak of them again. The ground is a lattice of failed grav mounts and warped frames, each plate stamped with dates and serials no one in New Atlantis admits exist, and Rivet has threaded himself through that history like a live wire. He has been stripping these carcasses for parts, building one last test frame and rigging the yard with "lessons" to collapse around anyone who gets close, all while consolidating the telemetry and design logs that prove who really cut corners. If he completes his work here, the evidence disappears in a plume of twisted metal and decompressed air, and the pattern of quiet disasters he followed from a Ranger's field notes to this very graveyard becomes just another rumor spacers pretend not to remember: anonymous schematics on a dataslate in the dust, erased audits on Deimos, and a trail of ships saved or shattered by the same invisible hand.

Docking log, personal copy, in case this all disappears like the rest.  

We were only supposed to babysit a drifting support ship for the Trade Authority, run basic checks, sign off on the tow. No one said why the TA tag looked like it had been peeled and re-stuck three times, or why every cargo cradle smelled of burnt lubricant and welding flux. In the cargo spine I found a slab of hull plate with seams too clean for any station yard out here, over-braced like someone expected to take fire. The manifest claimed it was scrap. The crew chief just stared at it, then at me, and changed the subject.  

Funny thing is, a few months back I rotated through an old UC relay where the consoles were full of ghost returns, unregistered work barges popping in and out of junk fields. The tech on duty swore it was sensor drift, then whispered later that the signatures had showed up before, always on routes that suddenly became very profitable for "the right people." Everybody talks like they have it all figured out in the mess, but the moment you suggest putting it in a report, the room goes quiet.

Dock's quiet now. Just the relay hum and the way the bulkheads creak when the rock flexes. Feels like the whole module is leaning in, listening to see if I talk.

They say this tug pilot never fires a shot. Ships just arrive light, containers written off, everyone shrugs and files the claim. I have seen the gaps behind those shrugs. Partial manifests that do not match hull capacity. Time stamps edited by a shaky hand. Credit transfers routed through dead accounts that somehow still pass Trade Authority checks.

Today a spacer brought me another fragment, said it came off a crate that "never existed." Same route vector I saw on that corrupted record from the research outpost, same ghost ping that bounced off an old relay nobody admits is active. All of it points to the same kind of place: where cargo goes to be forgotten before someone like her makes it useful again.

I am not stupid enough to say the name in the open channel, but I know which depot she has been bleeding dry. Nobody here knows the whole story. We just pass pieces along to people we trust to live long enough to use them.

The Well is close, crowded, and loud enough to hide the kind of questions I need to ask. Down there, the stories come wrapped in debt and old favors; people talk because they owe someone, or because they hate someone more than they fear MacLeod. If his name is written anywhere official, it is in the gaps between payments, the mismatched cargo tallies, the shifts nobody wants to remember working. Stepping into that maze means dealing with dockside politics and quiet threats, but the payoff could be the whole network laid bare on a single, dirty backroom slate.\n\nThe moonside relay is colder in every sense. Fewer eyes, longer shadows, and a broker who already flinched when my last questions grazed the truth. Out there, the noise is lower and the lies are easier to isolate against the hum of the reactor. The manifests running through that place are already too neat, too rehearsed; if I press hard enough, something will crack, and the spine of this smuggling line might light up clear as a navigation grid. Higher risk if the broker decides to warn him, but cleaner, sharper answers if he does not.

I am recording this from the relay bunker, in case someone needs to know why I walked back into a dead grid. The air still smells like old ozone and coolant, like the place is one power spike from remembering it mattered. I pulled the deserter's stolen scans off a buried buffer, the ones no one filed because they were easier to ignore than explain. Same patrol, same sweep pattern, but there is a shadow in the upper atmosphere that does not match any registered transponder, holding position right above that forgotten station on the ridge. It is all there in the timestamps and angles; you can almost feel the course corrections, like someone threading a needle through a gap the charts say does not exist. Maybe it is safer for everyone if that kind of flying stays a rumor, but pretending we never saw it is how we got here in the first place. The last listening post gave us ghost readings that did not line up with the public lanes, the deserter confirmed a ship cutting through restricted sky on a path nobody admits is real, and now the numbers point straight back to that same quiet station, waiting.

HopeTown means faces, voices, and the kind of lies that sweat through coveralls. If I walk into that yard asking after a nameless freighter from Montara, I will get shrugs, half-truths, and maybe a wrench across the back of my skull. But it is also where the paper trail breathes, where credits changed hands and someone decided to bolt war-grade metal onto a farmhand's ship. If I can pry that story loose from the people who lived it, I might finally understand who Dustback is protecting and why no one will say his name.\n\nThe drifting cache is cleaner, in its way. Cold vacuum, no dockside politics, just jammed buffers and manifests that never got the courtesy of a proper purge. The Specterborn prowling around it complicates things, but that hull is not there by accident; someone trusted the emptiness to finish a job they were too nervous to sign off on. Crack it open, and I get the version of events nobody had time to massage, the raw path of a hauler slipping off the grid toward sick soil and frightened settlements. One path talks, the other shows. I do not have the luxury of taking both at once.

Gagarin means noise, people, and too many ways to disappear in plain sight. If Vector spliced herself into the power grid, the proof is hiding under layers of cheap fixes and corporate upgrades. Following that thread is slow work: crawling conduits, bribing line techs, hoping whatever UC worker started this map did not vanish because they were onto something lethal. The payoff is a structural picture of the whole route, not just where she went, but how she has been riding the veins of this system.\n\nThe relay bunker is the opposite: empty, honest, and already half-forgotten by the people who built it. Those atmospheric scans do not care who signed what contract or who needed a favor buried; they just record what passed overhead. If someone pulled a copy and walked away spooked, it means the pattern in those flight paths points somewhere the charts say does not exist. Going back there is riskier in a different way. Less cover, more chance the wrong analyst notices I am sifting through erased history, but if I am right, one clean line from sky to that hidden corridor could cut through all the rumor.

I keep replaying the last jump profile in my head, like if I stare at the numbers long enough they will admit what we all refuse to say out loud. The Trustsphere should not be here, cold and torn open on a lane that was sold to us as safer than dockside. I walked past a hundred holo-ads in New Atlantis promising that GalBank watches over its investments like family; funny how none of those clips show a vault deck vented to vacuum. The nav buffers are scarred with corrections that are too elegant to be accidents, little nudges lining us up with someone's private kill box. When I took this side contract out of that busted quarter on Akila, it was supposed to be a clean audit, a chance to prove to my old crew I still had a future. I tagged the corrupted chains, flagged the inconsistencies, left a note to myself that I would come back with proper tools and a clearer head. I never did. If anyone finds this, know that the pattern started with a cheap dataslate in the dirt and angry spacers muttering about discount routes; it led here, to a dead protection ship that proves the odds were never on our side.

I thought this would be another dead end like the rest of my assignments out here, one more "monitor and report" buried under nicer words. The outpost is barely more than a sealed room, a crackling comm dish, and a bunk that smells like whoever had it before me smoked in their sleep. Still, the relay hears everything the lanes whisper past. Today, buried inside routine telemetry and a half-corrupted freighter ping, I caught it again: that same fractional drift in the jump solutions, the same signature from a skiff we lost six months back when Command told me my timestamps were off. I only saw it because Ops sent the wrong filter profile, the deck tech typoed a ship ID, and I forgot to purge yesterday's buffer. A chain of small mistakes no one will ever admit. Crossed with that old LIST incident file I was told to "deprioritize," it all folds toward a scrapyard orbiting Deimos that somehow features in traffic patterns way above its importance. So far I have a trail of dismissed reports, an anonymous tip from a nervous hauler, and now a set of lane deviations all curving toward the same patch of rust.

The PX-3446 hangs dead in the dark, a UC SysDef hull that should have been quietly towed and buried but instead left drifting just outside the busy lanes, where only someone following the wrong kind of math would think to look. Inside, the blast-sheared corridors and frozen fire doors say "training accident" to any official report, yet every sealed compartment hums with the sense of work interrupted just before it named a culprit. This is where field data and private suspicions were burned into the ship's memory banks, far from the committee rooms where admirals now swear they saw only random failures. The wreck is less a tomb than a locked filing cabinet, holding the one record of how Diego's patterns bled into military jumps, and why those who noticed chose to keep that knowledge in vacuum, not daylight. Up to now the trail has been whispers and half-truths: a dying captain's complaints on a forgotten rock, nervous route-sellers speaking off the record in a station bar, and scattered flight plans marked "mishap" that all shared the same quiet signature curling back to the same hand on the console.

I keep thinking if I say this out loud, it becomes real, so here it goes.

I ran manifests for a hauler out past New Atlantis, thought I knew how the numbers were supposed to look. Then we picked up that stray slate in the drift, all mismatched dates and dead transponders, pointing back to Trade Authority traffic it had no business knowing about. I laughed it off until I checked a personal account and half my life was suddenly "under review."

By the time I reached the city branch, the clerk downstairs swore my file had always been like that. Same tone at every window, the same little pauses when they read my name. Even the lawyer I found in the lower levels said there had been "another version" of my case once, but whatever it was got folded into rumor and bar talk a long time ago. Now I am sitting in the dark of this support ship, listening to its cooling metal, and the shape of it all is starting to show; quiet edits in station ledgers, cargo that moved without moving, and a whisper that the first person who tried to explain it disappeared from the records before anyone wrote down what they saw.

I am recording this from a borrowed bunk on a UC combat hull, and the hum here is wrong. Too clean. On my ship you could feel the drive's heartbeat through the soles of your boots, a little off-tempo, like it knew it was living on favors and hand-fit parts. They brought me aboard after the incident to "clarify my testimony," then parked me in a cold corridor while officers argued in a room I was not allowed to see. One of them slipped, mentioned a cryo facility well off-chart, then shut up when he saw I was listening. Later, a junior tech let me glance at a routing trace. Same coordinates we had been warned never to jump anywhere near, buried under layers of classification and "need to know." Whoever was supposed to chase that line left in a hurry; their duffel is still under the bunk opposite mine, folded uniforms never issued, slate blinking with an unfinished note. They told me to wait while they "verified a few things." That was three days and two course corrections ago, and the ship keeps drifting closer to those dead coordinates as if someone forgot to cancel an order nobody wants to admit was given.

I am recording this mostly so I can convince myself later that I did not imagine it.

The outpost is dead in all the obvious ways. Air smells like dust and coolant, screens dark, lab benches stripped. But the Lima Devils keep drifting through like they grew up here, stepping around certain doors without looking, using the same two jokes about "old science ghosts" and studiously not mentioning anything else. I asked one of them who used to run this place and he laughed, then froze, then said he "forgot" and changed the subject so fast it was almost clumsy. Thing is, the walls remember better than they do. Scratches where warning signs used to hang, faded tape outlines on the floor around equipment no one wants to describe, a schedule still pinned to a board with whole shifts blacked out instead of erased. 

Feels like everybody agreed, quietly, to stop recalling the details at the same time. Like names, dates, whole accidents just slid into a hole that someone dug on purpose. And now there is me, alone in the corridor, trying to decide whether following that gap in their memory is brave, or just stupid.

I am recording this because if I say it out loud again in the mess, they will just tell me I am reading ghosts into the traffic reports.

We were supposed to be running standard courier hops, comfortable little arcs between stations where the biggest worry is whose crate of snack packs leaks first. Then the route updates started coming in with gaps. Whole segments of flight plans redacted, replaced by neat, anonymous vectors threading right through places every pilot I know calls cursed weather. Ask who plotted them and people stop saying names. They tap the console, shrug toward orbit, talk about "the contractor" or "that navigator" like the sound might bite.

Trade Authority likes its deniability tidy. As long as the manifests balance and the couriers return, no one asks why the sensor feeds splice mid-storm. But I have seen the same signature in three different log sets now, a little pattern in the corrections like someone tightening screws in our sky. It feels like we are flying inside someone else's experiment, and the only time anyone mentions the architect, it is with a tilt of the chin, not a word.

Out here, the rock itself hums with the residue of what he has been doing. The mining complex was never built to host Grav Drive arrays, yet the shafts run straight into dense veins that bend readings, masking field tests from distant UC sensors and Freestar patrols alike. In these tunnels he can hide unstable prototypes between loaders and ore hoppers, burn stolen fuel, and dump irradiated slag into the walls while the workers call it a bad day in the drills. This is where his pattern converges where every anomalous route, every missing crate, every grav spike along the hauler lanes finally points. By the time the alarms trip, he will be one trigger pull from erasing the last proof of his part in the tender misjump and stepping fully into the shadows he helped Rhys open. The earliest version of how this began has already been traded away in bar stories and half wiped logs, but the trail is clear enough now remote datapads with scrambled signatures, a silent recorder drifting in orbit, hushed talk in a farming settlement, and a bruised asteroid field full of broken echoes all narrowing toward this buried heart.

Common Watch is the informal name given to the loose convoy of haulers, tugs, and survey cutters that habitually work the lanes around the derelict GC-5222 Stockwind. Originally a rotation of contract escorts keeping scavengers off GalBank traffic, the group has since grown into a semi-regular presence, trading drift warnings, selling updated debris charts, and quietly charging for "eyes-on" patrols when official coverage thins out.  \n\nTheir reputation is mixed: captains praise their vigilance, while more cynical traders claim Common Watch only sounds the alarm when there is no profit in staying quiet. One archived traffic control log notes a brief halt in their patrol while the crews burned minutes searching for a missing mug someone swore had been left on the main console, accompanied by open-band grumbling about how they lose the same junk every week out here. In that same exchange, a senior voice can be heard wondering aloud whether their old ritual of circling the drifting Stockwind at the start of each shift still means anything, or if they keep doing it only because no one wants to be the first to stop.

The skymaps all say this mining pit should be quiet rock and thin air, yet the clouds above it twist like something half-tamed and half-feral, caught between vacuum and storm. Stormglass chose this scar in the crust for a reason: the drills already pierce deep seams, the Helium-3 lines and old grav infrastructure hum beneath the surface, and the thin atmosphere responds faster than any regulated world. Here she can fold every lesson and every mistake into one last experiment, trying to rewrite the hyperstorm that ruined her life by bleeding reactor exhaust and microclimate tweaks into the open sky. A single miscalculated correction from her early models turned one settlement into a grave; left alone, what she is forcing through the rock and air here could echo across systems.  \nWe traced her from a stray dataslate in the back end of nowhere to Ranger logs and worried technicians at a supply post, then through a strained Helium-3 facility running odd atmospheric diagnostics and a raider command site choked in storm-scoured rubble; every step pointed to the same pattern of tampered skies and abandoned safeguards.

Filed on a dead shift, because nobody reads these unless something explodes.

I have been staring at the same stack of incident reports all week. Broken loaders, bad weather, bar fights out by the farms. Noise. Then I started cross-tagging the implant failures the way nobody pays me to do, and the noise turned into an echo. Same firmware fragment, same off-the-books installer, same shrug from every clinic that signed the contracts.

Today I pulled a robotics maintenance ticket for a site that is supposed to be mothballed. Power draw says otherwise. Parts orders rerouted there line up with the dates of those seizures planetside. When I mentioned it in the mess, the room went quiet in that special way, where people stop saying certain names and just tap their fingers on the table instead. So I logged the coordinates, flagged the lab in my own notes, and locked this entry where it will not be auto-archived into nothing. If anyone actually follows up, they will find their next step in that forgotten complex, where dead machines are learning new tricks from someone who knows exactly how to vanish between signatures.

Neon's Underbelly is the obvious move: follow the stink. If Vector is bleeding off grav sins anywhere, it is down there in the steam and rust, where waste, chems, and people all get flushed through the same veins. It will be noisy, crowded, too many eyes and not enough law, but that cuts both ways. I can lean on Ghost Coil types, bribe a few maintenance crews, see who has been paid to look away when the wrong pipes light up. Messy, dangerous, and close enough to the source that I might feel the Echo in the walls.\n\nThe research module is cleaner, quieter, and a different kind of trap. Here the story is written in routing tables and aborted transfers, the kind of thing that never makes dockside gossip but shapes entire shipping lanes. If Vector carved his own corridor through corporate sims, this is where the first cuts were made. Digging there means sifting through someone's carefully curated lies, maybe stepping on Ryujin toes, maybe tripping alarms meant for data thieves, not hunters. Less blood, more ghosts in the code, but if I unravel the fork he tampered with, I might see exactly which way he is steering next.

HopeTown is the honest face of the lie. If I walk those gantries, I am walking through the last place families saw as "safe," talking to loaders who still sleep fine because they never see where the ships actually end up. The risk here is soft: backroom conversations, forged signatures, LIST clerks who will close ranks the second they smell an audit. But if I can peel back their paperwork, I might finally see who signed off on letting him rewrite entire lives with a few quiet keystrokes.\n\nThe depot is the ugly side of the same story. Out here, fuel and timing are the only truths that cannot be sweet-talked away. The people guarding those tanks are not administrators; they are scavengers and cut-rate muscle who know exactly how many tons vanish off the books when no one is looking. Going in means noise, maybe blood, and whatever passes for loyalty among crews who live on kickbacks and "lost" shipments. Still, the numbers on their ledgers are closer to his hand than any brochure in HopeTown, and if I want to see where his perfect corridor really bends, following the burn trail through them might be the faster, sharper cut.

The Well is where forgotten things are supposed to sink and stay down, drowned beneath tourist gloss and MAST rhetoric. Down here, records get lost, debts get rolled into shadows, and faces blur into the press of the crowd. For a man who lives by erasing people on paper, this undercity is the perfect last staging ground, close enough to GalBank's veins to tap them, low enough that no one in the towers wants to look too hard. He has been threading everything toward this point, consolidating false identities, liquidating hijacked claims, and preparing to cut loose from the Settled Systems with a ledger wiped clean. The quietly reassigned freighters in the drift, the altered case files beneath the plazas, the corrupted manifests hidden in Trade Authority holds were all pieces of the same exit strategy. Someone in the core tried to smother what they found, but the story kept leaking through bar talk and ruined captains. From that first stray dataslate in the black, to the nervous clerk in the city above, to the corrupted support ship parked off the main lanes, every whisper has led back to this pressure sink under New Atlantis.

I am writing this down because if I say it out loud again, somebody will tell me to lay off the chems or get back to work. The lab should be dead. Power grid cut years ago, no traffic, no reason for anything out there to still hum. And yet that icebox glows on long-range like a bad tooth, and every time a hauler skirts its sky my console shows the same microscopic bend in their descent. Pilots blame weather, controllers blame worn sensors, command shrugs and files another "unexplained fluctuation."\n\nOff-duty, in the mess, you still hear the old stories. A Navy run that vanished after a routine ping. A convoy that never made the farmstead. Each tale told softer than the last, like everyone hopes if they whisper low enough the numbers will stop lining up. They have shuffled the reports, retired the officers, buried the families in condolences and statistics, but the pattern keeps bleeding through. I am not special; I just sat one watch too many with the scopes turned up and the volume down, and now I cannot unsee that all those missing ships seem to tip their wings over the same patch of frozen nowhere before they disappear.

I keep telling myself I only came to Neon for cheap parts and cheaper drinks, but I have been stuck in Ebbside three nights now, listening to pipes instead of music. The walls here sweat, little beads along the conduits, and every time the pressure drops the whole bar goes quiet for half a heartbeat. Folks pretend it is nothing, then start talking louder.

Dockhands swear the taps ran clean yesterday and sour today, that tankers dock at hours no one remembers logging. I saw a maintenance panel half-open in a service corridor, tools laid out just so, like somebody got called away mid-job and never came back to finish the tidy work. No lock, no seal, just that low hum through the metal and the taste of iron on the air.

I checked that corrupted slate I picked up out past nowhere, then listened to a drunk spacer mutter the same intake codes in his sleep. Different places, same feeling. Someone was supposed to smooth this over, file the reports, pretend the water still flows like it should. Instead, the mess is just sitting here, humming behind thin walls, waiting for someone stubborn or stupid enough to start pulling at it.

The Abandoned Bionics Lab sits at the end of every line you have pulled, a dead facility with live power and just enough automated systems left for someone like her to bend into a private theater. Here the tools are already in the walls: surgical bays, dormant prosthetic rigs, and half-coded interface suites she can wake with a keystroke, all buried far from regulators and still wired to old Ryujin standards she helped design. Out here she can finish stitching together the network hinted at in stolen firmware archives and smuggling ledgers, using the last intact equipment to tune a free mesh that would slip past any corporate leash, then ghost away behind her augmented clients. The scorched access door and a half-completed breach charge suggest another crew tried to end this and never made it past the first line of defenses. So far the trail reads like this: a forgotten dataslate in the back of beyond, ghost references to missing neuroamp designs in a quiet research outpost, then this same lab half-lit and full of erased logs, pointing to Splice circling back to weaponize the only place that still remembers how to build her.

I used to joke I could fly a SysDef hull blind just by the hum in the deckplates. PX-15 feels the same as every other combat frame I've patched on, same scuffed corridors, same stale TerraBrew in the galley, same officers treating techs like background noise. That is the problem. When you know every panel by heart, you stop questioning the ones that do not belong. I saw the first altered jump projections three shifts ago, tucked in among old interdiction charts. Thought some junior analyst had fat-fingered a waypoint, so I corrected it and moved on. Now I keep finding the same pattern, mirrored, inverted, threaded through legacy threat maps like someone stitching a new spine into dead data. Back on that dustball relay, there was a trader whispering about missing convoys and a name I had heard in The Well years before, buried in LIST chatter. I remember thinking it was all rumor. Then PX-15 turned up on my assignment list, tagged routine archival work, and I signed off without a second glance. Familiar callsigns, familiar procedures, and somewhere in that comfort, a whole new route was slipped past everyone who should have seen it.

I have worked manifests for the Trade Authority long enough to know when the numbers are lying.

On their own, they all looked clean. A crate here routed one system wider than it needed to be, a refuel stop added to a hauler that should have had the range, a timing window that cut it a little close to a patrol schedule. You shrug, you blame lazy clerks or overcautious captains, and you sign where you are told to sign.

Then one evening on the cargo deck I laid three runs side by side, all from different shippers, all stamped months apart. Same "optional" detour, same quiet refuel station, same gap in recorded telemetry. It felt like staring at a face I had seen a dozen times on passing crowds but never really looked at.

People whisper about someone who can sell you a route that slips between all the cracks. I used to laugh that off. Lately it feels like we have been freighting ghost footprints for him. The last batch of manifests I checked before we lost contact with the Starborne had that same detour buried in the route code. Coincidence stops feeling like chance when it starts repeating in the same cold, careful handwriting.

This part of Akila is where ships come to die slow, and the people who worked them are not far behind, which is exactly why any talk worth hearing sinks into the rust instead of floating up to the Core. Between leaning shacks and crooked repair stalls, actuators and grav rings pile in heaps, tagged with half-legible IDs from haulers that vanished on routes no insurance adjuster wants to audit too closely. The junction buried under all this clutter is not just scrap; it is a scar from a job that went wrong in a very specific way, a place where someone tested how far they could bend a flight path before it snapped. To pick through it here, at the edge of polite notice, is to step into a conversation every spacer in this quarter pretends they are not having, their words clipped short and eyes sliding away whenever timing, discounts, or a certain unseen navigator come up. So far, all you have are a half-burned dataslate from a forgotten camp and low-voiced rumors from worn-out haulers, enough to suggest that some jumps are being nudged off true and that the same quiet signature keeps surfacing wherever wreckage and bad luck pile together.

I am starting to think the worst damage on a SysDef ship never shows up on a hull scan. It is in the tiny gaps between what one person meant to say and what the next person actually heard. Naomi Khatri swore she logged the last change to our patrol lanes; Leah Ortiz insists she never saw it. Erin Cho thought Command's burst about "legacy triage assets" was just another dead file bouncing around the network. I thought the medic they flagged was a ghost story to keep us sharp on watch.\n\nToday, HM-7378 dropped out exactly where the amended orders said to, only to find a medical courier wreck that is not on any official chart and a string of reroutes buried under half a decade of "we will fix it later." Comms traffic does not quite line up with the nav logs, and nobody can explain why our previous shift burned three hours loitering off a rock that does not appear in the briefing. None of it is big enough on its own to raise an alarm, but all together it feels like we have been nudged, a few degrees at a time, into someone else's forgotten emergency response. If this is just a paperwork snarl, it is the most elaborate one I have ever seen.

Some nights I think half the Settled Systems lives off lies told in cargo bars. Gagarin is proof. Every time I ask about those lost convoys I get a different version, sanded smooth by whoever is talking. Dock clerks swear the lanes were straight and certified. Haulers over Erdebrau insist the routes kinked at the last second into the same patch of bad sky. No one ever agrees on details, just on one thing; it was not their fault. You can feel it in the way the story edges keep getting rounded off, like they have all told it too many times to themselves already.\n\nI started copying manifest numbers on the sly, lining them up against what little GalBank will still show, and the more I look the less the official record matches what people mutter in backrooms. Insurance spikes on runs that were supposedly uneventful. Traffic traces that look like someone took a handful of convoys and nudged them, just a little, onto the same strange three-forked pattern. Nobody wants to say the name tied to those adjustments out loud, but when it does slip through their teeth, it comes out soft, like they are afraid he might be listening on an open channel.

I was not supposed to take the job. Should have left that low-grade Alliance posting to some green kid with a patched suit and big dreams. But a derelict signaling from nowhere smells like clean salvage, and clean salvage pays.  

The shuttle was wrong the second I saw it. Hull creased in directions metal does not like to bend, cockpit torn open from the inside, like the jump itself had tried to eat its way out. I buried what was left of the pilot with my gloves still on, dust clinging to the suit, then found his slate half-melted under a rock he had not finished stacking.  

There was enough data left to scrape together a name, the same one I heard once in a bar on Gagarin when freighter captains got too drunk to watch their tongues. Short, sharp, the way spacers talk about storms. Nav noise on his last jump matched an old ghost blip I logged years back and forgot, filed under sensor glitch to keep dispatch off my back.  

Funny how the past leaves fingerprints on the present. One bad reading ignored, one rumor laughed off, and suddenly the lines all converge on a single path someone has been penciling into the dark for a long time.

I keep replaying that day on the outpost like a bad grav sim with a glitching reset. It was supposed to be routine: check the soil monitors, log the yields, complain about funding over cold TerraBrew. I saw the anomaly in the routing table, a little flag on a grain shipment that did not match the standard template. I remember thinking, "must be some clerk in Gagarin fat-fingering codes again," and I let it sit until after lunch.

By then the recall order had appeared and vanished in the queue, just a flicker. The samples still went out.

I told myself it was nothing, that people above my pay grade knew what they were doing. Then reports started drifting back months later, in rumor not in data: colonists coughing up dust, fields that would not stop producing even after the farmers begged for a fallow cycle. Someone down the chain kept calling it a miracle. Someone up the chain kept insuring it. I keep wondering if I had overridden that single shipment, forced a manual review, whether any of this would still be happening, or if they would have just found another technician too tired to double-check a harmless little deviation in the code.

I keep telling myself it is coincidence.

One farmer comes in, says his arm rig locked during harvest. Glitch, fine. Next week a hauler swears her vision implant fuzzed out right as she hit orbit. Different clinic, different brand, same shrug from the rep on the other end of the line. I log it, because that is what I do out here in the tin box while the real decisions get made in cities I will never see.

Then the numbers start to rhyme.

Same fragment in the diagnostics, same vague reference to an "independent tech," same way people drop their eyes when I ask who did the install. They stop saying names, start pointing with their chins, like the old days when you did not say a gang's tag out loud. The complaints get marked resolved upstairs, but they keep walking through my door, shaking, scared, angry.

Tonight I laid the reports out on the desk and followed dates and coordinates with my finger until the trail curled back on itself. Too many accidents lining up on the same curve for me to call it bad luck anymore. Coincidences stacked until they leaned, and once they leaned they pointed, and now I cannot pretend I do not see where.

I think this is still the Ananke Drift, but the nav keeps flickering like it does not want to admit we are really here. Suits me fine. No one likes logging this rock anyway.

Met the Aegis man today. He did not say Aegis, but you can hear it in the way he measures every word, like he is still on record even when his badge is gone. Face looked like he had not slept since the coolant incident everyone avoids naming directly. Ask three people what happened and you get three stories, all framed to make sure no one in uniform comes back with questions. Nobody pushes too hard; out here, curiosity is just a slower way to die.

He handed me a cracked slate, said he was "done chasing ghosts." The trace on it is not a ghost, though. It is a route signature, buried under maintenance pings and survey sweeps, repeating at intervals that match a very real ship. I crosschecked it with what little I have: that stray dataslate from the fringe homestead, the harvest that grew too well, and the way a certain name keeps surfacing in dockside rumors whenever someone mentions miracle grain and missing logs. Wherever that pattern leads next, it is not random.

I am done pretending this is random.

When I took this posting on the rock, it was supposed to be easy time. Push manifests, skim a little off the top, sign whatever the system fed me. Then the "variance" jobs started showing up. Same ship classes, same lanes, always shifted a hair off the standard corridor. Escorts dropped by just one hull. Refuel stops quietly deleted. First one, I thought the clerk before me was lazy. Fifth one, I told myself the computer was glitching. Twentieth, and my hands were shaking every time I hit confirm.

Tonight I dug deeper. Buried in the routing tables was an old UC code woven through the edits, a reference tag that should not exist on a backwater module like this. I followed it, line by line, until it pointed at a forgotten military node out-system, one of those posts they "decommissioned" on paper and left to rot in the dust. All my altered lanes bend toward it, like someone has been curving traffic around a blind spot for years and paying idiots like me to press the button.

I thought I was just helping cargo dodge fees and inspections. Turns out I have been nudging people onto a board I cannot even see.

This outpost was never meant to matter; just another research shell on a quiet rock, built for routine data pulls and then half forgotten as priorities drifted elsewhere. That is what makes it perfect for what she did to it. When departments shifted, staff rotated, and oversight thinned to the occasional automated ping, the traffic through here kept flowing on old schedules, half monitored and half ignored. Somewhere in that slow slide from purpose to neglect, someone rewired a single exchange a handshake that once just synced survey results now brushes past LIST archives, Trade Authority ledgers, and settlement queues before vanishing into blank space. If I can pry open what is left of that link, I can see which chains she broke on purpose and which ones she quietly grafted together. Up to now all I have are scattered signs a dead end contact who asked the wrong question, a sealed lab with its logs scrubbed too clean, a nervous broker on Neon fencing partial routes, a derelict survey cutter with half a jump plan and every fragment points to her carefully bending systems over time, until nobody remembers what they were built to do in the first place.

I keep replaying that survey run in my head, the one that brought us down to this nobody rock. We were behind schedule, two drones already fried by static, so when the air samplers started flashing out-of-range, I just tagged the readings as localized contamination and pushed on. No budget for curiosity. We scraped a few cores, logged coordinates, lifted before the storm front ate the landing gear.  

Weeks later, back on the station, those same samples showed a pattern that did not match any refinery waste or colony runoff. A precise kind of wrong, like someone had been drawing lines through the atmosphere with a scalpel. I filed a note to Environmental, then watched it vanish under "non-critical." Ships kept jumping through the sector, captains grumbling about minor course corrections, nothing more.  

Now I have seen the half-burned log from that outpost, heard the nervy chatter about a freighter that never arrived, and skimmed the vault ship manifests that almost make sense if you ignore the gaps. It feels like whatever she did down there started as a rushed test, a small cheat in the math, and we all stepped over the stain without looking down.

I keep telling myself the array is just old hardware and lazy clerks, but sitting in this cramped console seat, listening to the static between pings, it feels more like I am eavesdropping on a lie everyone agreed not to talk about. The corridor it watches is not on any chart I can pull without favors, yet the sensors know it is there; tiny grav spikes, ships sliding through at angles that make my stomach tighten just looking at the vector math. Traffic control tagged them as calibration drift years ago and then, somehow, never circled back. Funny how nobody quite remembers who filed the original note, or why the budget never stretched far enough to decommission the array outright. I have seen that same silence before: at a frontier dock where a captain "lost" half his jump logs, in a station bar where people changed the subject as soon as Neon's power dips came up, in a maintenance bay where a tech swore she had never met a pilot named Vector but could trace his burns on the hulls she patched. Now this old watcher is staring straight down the throat of a path he is been rehearsing, and every omission around it feels less like ignorance and more like consent.

Funny how the story keeps changing, depending who is telling it and how close they are to a docking bay. First time I heard it, over watered whiskey in the mess, it was just a rumor about a liner that came apart mid jump, no names, no blame, just a bad roll of the grav dice. Next station over, the same tale had a villain, some engineer who signed off on cheap steel and vanished into the black. After that, I kept hearing about a shadow on the docks, a quiet tech who slipped aboard at night and fixed what the staryards pretended not to see.\n\nToday I ended up in that crooked little Freestar trailer at the edge of the pad, listening to a deputy whose hands shook just a little when they scrolled through failure reports. Same incidents, same ship classes, same manufacturer tags, but the way they talked about it was different: not curses, not campfire stories, just a pattern no one higher up wanted to acknowledge. They say the masked fixer is a saboteur in one port, a savior in another. The only thing that does not change is the silence whenever someone asks why the same hulls keep cracking in the same way and why the logs keep getting buried under other case numbers.

I am writing this down so I will not start believing the official version.

We were three ships running ore and machine parts toward HopeTown, nothing fancy, same corridor I have flown since before the Armistice. UC traffic pings in a correction, minor variance, cleaner path through the junk belt. I swear I checked the vector twice. Looked safe. Then we caught the echo of a wreck ahead that should not have been there, hull still warm on thermals, cargo already stripped clean. Somebody had got the tip before us rode the same correction, just a few hours earlier.

Afterward, in the bar at New Atlantis, the story turned into one more spacer tale bad luck, old charts, UC underfunding. The captains laughed it off, but when the drinks thinned out, they started whispering about a voice that sounds like ops, numbers that never show in the logs. Every time the rumor cooled, some tug limped in with a new near miss and the same quiet pattern, like the story is trying to die and keeps getting dragged back up by people who cannot unsee their own telemetry. I am no investigator. I just know my ship went exactly where I was told to go, and someone was already there, waiting.

I am writing this in the dark between shifts, because the ship feels wrong and I do not trust the official logs to remember that. We were not supposed to break route this close to Neon. Manifest said standard haul, no deviations, but the Trade Authority dispatcher slipped in a new vector at the last minute, barely a line of explanation. The bridge took it anyway. Credits make people move faster than they should. Now the Skyclipper hums unevenly, like the Grav core is holding its breath, and half the nav data from the last jump came through smeared, as if the stars themselves dragged. Ivy tried to scrub the errors, muttering that it was just interference from traffic around Volii, but I saw the look she gave that corrupted segment, like it was something alive. Someone pushed this course in a hurry, then turned their eyes away from what it might brush against. Out on a survey outpost we found the first stray blackbox, just a fragment. Then there were those odd beacon returns in high orbit, callsigns that matched ships marked as lost, and now this cargo run with its quiet addendum and a route line that bends closer to Neon's shadows than any normal hauler would risk.

Hard to say when it started feeling inevitable. Maybe back on that rock out past the lanes, when I cracked open a discarded slate and saw numbers that did not belong to any homestead that size. Maybe in Gagarin, watching freight hands swear a shipment existed while the manifest swore it did not. Either way, it brought me here.

The Fundrunner is dead metal outside, but inside you can still feel the hum of old credit flows, like a ghost current under your boots. GalBank stamped their logo everywhere, as if repetition makes trust. It does not. Every sealed rack I pass smells like another story that ended the same way: someone in the black, someone in the ground.

The trail says whoever taught her how to cut debts loose used ships like this as a pulpit. Phantom yields at an extraction site that should be dry, families whose ledgers just blinked clean, a pattern of erased risk that always arcs back toward Helium-3 and quiet corridors like these. I followed rumors from a forgotten outpost to noisy docks, from there to this drifting vault, and every step made it clearer this was never random; the numbers were always steering me toward the plants that feed the whole game.

I am recording this quietly, because people who talk too loud about lanes and disappearances stop getting invited back on good contracts. Learned that the hard way at a bar outside HopeTown two months ago. I mentioned a transport that never pinged its arrival beacon, and three captains suddenly remembered somewhere else they had to be. The fourth just stared into his drink and told me, very carefully, that the frontier eats ships and stories the same way.\n\nToday I put down on an old relay they swore was decommissioned. No traffic, no maintenance drones, just a dead lattice hanging where three routes used to meet. Inside, the boards are burned but not empty; you can still see faint traces of jumps that do not match any published corridor. Someone carved their own path through here, again and again, so clean the drives barely left a bruise. I mentioned that pattern once to a LIST clerk I know, and watched her face close up like an airlock. She changed the subject to fuel prices and never answered my messages after. Out here, everyone has noticed something wrong in the map, but the smart ones keep their opinions small, like they are afraid the vacuum might be listening.

The Abandoned Deimos Scrapyard is where her whole crusade was always heading, a place built on the lie that wrecks are just metal and not the people written out of the manifests. Here, among gutted hulls and stripped grav drives, she is threading the last of her stolen data through hidden cores, preparing to erase or broadcast everything the salvage ring buried under "administrative resolutions." UC and Freestar patrols turned blind eyes to this yard for years, calling it obsolete while she turned it into a fortress and an archive in one. The rusted cranes, mined walkways, and jury-rigged turrets are not simply defenses but levers; if she finishes locking her ledgers here, the ghost-insured ships become more than rumor and the factions complicit in their loss may burn or double down. This is the last gap before the graveyards belong entirely to her or are swallowed again by the same silence that let her work go unnoticed for so long. So far, the trail has run from a discarded report in the dust to a sabotaged relay that throttled distress calls, then into a derelict UC combat ship whose untouched logs showed military routes overlapping "accidental" civilian disappearances.

Everybody swears they heard it from someone else first.

The deserter whose bunk I borrowed said a friend in SysDef mentioned it over cards. The tech running the power in this rusted hide said it came down from some analyst on Jemison. I am sitting in the dark with the last of the juice running through an old overwatch console, and no one will admit they were the one who actually saw it.

Thing is, I have seen it now.

Buried three layers down under scrubbed patrol logs, there is a jump trace that does not fit any sanctioned corridor. The ship on that feed slides between pings, just outside where the net is supposed to be solid, like it knows exactly where the blind spots live. Every time it reappears, its vector lines kiss the same set of coordinates orbiting Deepala. The Clinic.

People say that station sees everything the war broke and everything the lanes keep breaking still. If he is sampling the damage his numbers do, that is where he would go to listen. I have got the timestamp, the entry window, and the angle his drive flared when he dropped into local space. It is not much, but it is the first time this ghost leaves the same fingerprint in two different systems.

I keep telling myself this is just another relay job, just another Trade Authority courier drifting between people who pretend they are not on the same side. The hull hums like always, life support purrs, the recycler coughs every few hours. Familiar noises. Comforting, until you notice the other sounds.

Tonight I heard the ship talk to no one.

Old UC diagnostic routines, buried deep in the nav core, spun up during downtime. Their pings went out into the dark, calling to beacons that were supposed to be decommissioned years ago. No one on the manifest ordered that. The captain shrugged, said legacy code sometimes ghosts the system. But I watched the patterns scroll by and they were too clean, too deliberate, like somebody had been tuning them while we ran cargo and looked the other way.

We docked at a rock last week, quiet place, barely a name. A freelancer handed over a data packet, eyes flicking to the stars every other breath, muttering about ships that arrive late or not at all. Since then, the old routines have been waking more often, pointing toward the same patch of sky. The pay on this route is better than it should be. Everyone pretends not to notice that, either.

I am sitting in a dead relay, listening to ghosts that never got the memo war is over.

The main board is red-lit and half the panels are fused, but when I tied a microcell into the backbone, the grid woke up like it had just been on break. Old patrol routines, still cycling after all these years, quietly logging every shuttle and ore hauler that screamed past the no-fly line. Nobody checked, nobody cared, so the system kept watching.

Buried under a decade of dust and recycled timestamps, I found it  a set of atmospheric returns that did not match any filed transponder, cutting through restricted airspace like they owned it. The pattern is clean, too clean for a smuggler guessing blind. Whoever plotted that path knew every blind arc in the grid and trusted the forgotten software to still be doing its job. I piggybacked the trajectory into orbitals and there it was, a residual signature stitched into traffic corrections around a processing hub hanging over the planet.  

So now I know where the next piece is waiting, caught in the same old procedures that outlived their operators. The brass turned their eyes away, but the machines never stopped watching, and she gambled on that.

I am writing this from the corner of the trailer, back to the bulkhead so I can see the door. The deputy went out for "fresh air," which is funny given the dust, and left their board on idle. They think I do not notice where their eyes slide whenever the subject comes up, how the room goes quiet when someone mentions that engineer in anything louder than a mutter. Nobody wants to be the one on record knowing too much.\n\nStill, patterns are hard to unsee once you trace them. Every jump failure, every emergency dock closure, every "miracle" overnight repair the deputy flagged sits on the same crooked line. The last report they filed, buried under a different case number, mentions a disposal site Deimos supposedly cleared years ago. Same prefix code on the ship that limped in last month with stress fractures on a frame that was "well within spec." They circled those coordinates twice, then closed the file without sending it.
